unit: publication date of the Wall Street Journal profile of Dario and Daniela Amodei
note: 'The Brother-Sister Duo Who Want to Keep Anthropic Weird' (WSJ, 21 November 2026, paywalled); Techmeme's summary: 'while at OpenAI, Dario suggested immersive videogames might ease political strife from AI-induced joblessness'; other reports attribute the remark to widely circulated Slack messages

unit: views of the most viewed X post spreading the report (about 5.6 million)
note: post of 22 November 2026 by a company account; view count read on 26 November 2026 through X search; the essay does not check the posts

unit: studies with quantitative evidence on cash transfers and spending on alcohol and tobacco (44 estimates), plus 11 studies that asked recipients
period: studies from 1997 to early 2014, Latin America, Africa and Asia
note: 'This paper reviews 19 studies with quantitative evidence on the impact of cash transfers on temptation goods, as well as 11 studies that surveyed the number of respondents who reported they used transfers for temptation goods. Almost without exception, studies find either no significant impact or a significant negative impact' (Evans and Popova, World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 6886, May 2014, abstract; Economic Development and Cultural Change 65(2), 2017)

unit: of the 44 estimates: negative and significant, negative and not significant, positive and not significant, positive and significant (82% negative)
note: 'there are 12 estimates which are negative and significant, 24 which are negative and insignificant, 6 which are positive and insignificant, and 2 which are positive and significant ... 82% of estimates are negative'; the two positive results are weakly significant and not consistent within the same study (WPS 6886, section 4)

unit: USD PPP, average GiveDirectly transfer (at least USD 404 PPP; almost two years of per capita spending), 503 recipient households
note: Haushofer and Shapiro, Quarterly Journal of Economics 131(4), 2016, section II

unit: USD PPP a month more nondurable spending (comparison households in the same villages: USD 158 PPP); food USD 19 PPP more
period: about nine months after the transfers began
note: 'we observe an increase in monthly nondurable expenditure of $36 PPP relative to the spillover group mean of $158 PPP' (abstract of the author manuscript); 'With the exception of temptation goods (alcohol and tobacco), transfers increase expenditures in all categories' (Table V)

unit: USD PPP a month, effect on alcohol (control mean 6.38) and tobacco (control mean 1.52) spending, not significant
period: about nine months after the transfers began
note: Table V; 'The treatment effects on alcohol and tobacco expenditure are negative and insignificant, although a lack of power does not allow us to rule out reasonably sized increases'; a list randomization method also found no effect (Online Appendix Table 29)

unit: % rise in alcohol spending, the smallest the study could detect (minimum detectable effect, USD 2.78 PPP a month)
period: about nine months after the transfers began
note: 'For alcohol our MDE was $2.78 PPP per month, which is a 44% increase relative to the control group mean of $6.38 PPP'

unit: USD PPP more in asset holdings (control mean USD 495 PPP)
period: about nine months after the transfers began

unit: USD a month to 1,000 low-income adults aged 21 to 40 in Illinois and Texas for three years; 2,000 in the control group received USD 50 a month
note: OpenResearch Unconditional Cash Study (Miller et al., NBER Working Paper 32711, abstract)

unit: USD a month more total spending (control mean USD 3,979); food USD 67, rent USD 52, car payments and insurance USD 30, gifts or loans to family and charity USD 22 (almost 26%)
period: during the three years of transfers
note: Table 4 and section text of Bartik, Rhodes, Broockman, Krause, Miller and Vivalt, 'The Impact of Unconditional Cash Transfers on Consumption and Household Balance Sheets: Experimental Evidence from Two US States', NBER Working Paper 32784 (August 2024, revised September 2026); also OpenResearch, Key Findings: Spending (21 July 2024)

unit: USD a month more on alcohol, tobacco, marijuana and gambling (control mean USD 138), significant at the 10% level only
period: during the three years of transfers
note: 'spending on "vice" goods, such as alcohol, tobacco, drugs, and gambling do not rise notably more than other spending categories in either dollars or as a percent of the control mean. In total, spending on these vice goods only rises by about $13 per month, or a little over 1% of the total transfer' (NBER WP 32784, revised September 2026)

unit: USD a month more on recreation and entertainment (control mean USD 51) and on vacations and trips (control mean USD 80)
period: during the three years of transfers

unit: days without drinking alcohol in the last 30 days, effect (control mean 27.24); total drinks in the last 30 days +0.978 (control mean 9.56), not significant
period: surveys during the three years of transfers
note: Table 12 of Miller, Rhodes, Bartik, Broockman, Krause and Vivalt, 'Does Income Affect Health? Evidence from a Randomized Controlled Trial of a Guaranteed Income', NBER WP 32711 (July 2024, revised August 2026): drinking more often and less interference with responsibilities are significant at the 10% level only and none survives the FDR adjustment; 'we also do not find evidence of harmful effects of the transfer on the abuse of drugs and alcohol that some may have feared'

unit: USD a month for 24 months to 125 residents of Stockton, California, on a prepaid debit card
note: SEED, Preliminary Analysis: SEED's First Year (West, Castro Baker, Samra and Coltrera, March 2021)

unit: % of tracked card purchases, monthly average: food, sales/merchandise, utilities, auto care; less than 1% tobacco and alcohol
note: 'Less than 1% of tracked purchases were for tobacco and alcohol'; 'approximately 40% of the money loaded to the prepaid debit card was either transferred to a pre-existing bank account or withdrawn as cash' (pages 11 and 12)

unit: CAD, a one-off cash transfer to 50 people experiencing homelessness (65 controls), equal to British Columbia's annual income assistance in 2016
note: Dwyer, Palepu, Williams, Daly-Grafstein and Zhao, 'Unconditional cash transfers reduce homelessness', PNAS 120(36), e2222103120 (2023); participants were screened for non-severe substance use, alcohol use and mental health symptoms, a 31% screen-in rate

unit: fewer days homeless over one year; USD 1,160 more savings, USD 429 more spending a month; spending on alcohol, drugs and cigarettes not different; net societal savings of 777 per recipient
note: 'spending on temptation goods (i.e., alcohol, drugs, cigarettes) was not different between groups. Although spending was measured through self-reports'; analyses described as exploratory

unit: % of people aged 20 to 69 using the 2020 Special Cash Payment for living costs, savings, domestic travel; % who saved all of it
note: internet survey of 2,062 people, more than one answer allowed (NLI Research Institute, Naoko Kuga, 12 November 2021, in Japanese, figures 2 and 3); the survey asked about uses, not amounts
